lead: An optical receiver turns a weak, noisy pulse train of light into clean digital bits. Every bit period it must decide whether the light was on or off, and it must do so at a stated error rate using as little power as possible. The chain is fixed: photodiode, low-noise preamplifier, main amplifier and equaliser, low-pass filter, and a decision circuit clocked by a recovered timing signal. Its key specification is sensitivity, the weakest average power that still meets the target bit error rate. Every link budget in Unit 5 starts from this number.
prereq: You need: chapter 4.1 for responsivity and chapter 4.4 for the noise current σ.

sections.h3: The chain from photon to bit

blocks.text: A receiver does four jobs in order: convert light to current, amplify that current with as little added noise as possible, shape the pulses so each bit sits in its own time slot, and decide one or zero at the centre of each slot.

items: Photodiode: absorbs the light and delivers a current I = R·P, where R is the responsivity in A/W and P is the received optical power in W.
Preamplifier: a low-noise current-to-voltage stage. Its noise dominates the whole receiver.
Main amplifier and equaliser: raises the signal to a few volts and compensates pulse spreading from the fiber and the front end.
Low-pass filter: removes out-of-band noise. Its bandwidth is set near the bit rate so noise is limited without smearing the pulses.

Decision circuit: a comparator that samples the filtered signal at t = nT, where T = 1/B is the bit period, B is the bit rate and n is the bit index. It outputs one if the sample is above the threshold.
Timing recovery: extracts a clock at B from the data transitions and feeds it to the decision circuit. Without it the sample point drifts.
AGC: automatic gain control, a loop that holds the output level constant when the received power changes, so the threshold stays valid.

blocks.text: AGC matters because a receiver must work over a dynamic range, the ratio between the strongest and weakest power it accepts. Above the upper limit the amplifiers overload: pulses flatten and the receiver fails on strong signals, not weak ones.
The preamplifier choice fixes both bandwidth and noise.

blocks.text: In a transimpedance amplifier a resistor R_f sits in the feedback path of an inverting amplifier. The output is V = −I·R_f, so the transresistance equals R_f in ohms. A larger R_f raises the output and lowers the input-referred thermal noise current, which falls as √(4kT/R_f). The price is bandwidth.

blocks.where: B is the closed-loop bandwidth in Hz; R_f is the feedback resistance in Ω; C is the total input capacitance in F, from photodiode and amplifier.

blocks.text: Doubling R_f halves the noise current but halves the bandwidth. That trade-off is the whole design problem of the front end.
Sensitivity is the minimum average received optical power needed to reach a stated bit error rate at a stated bit rate. It is meaningless without both numbers attached.

blocks.where: P is the average optical power in W; P_dBm is the same power in decibel-milliwatts.

blocks.text: For a PIN receiver limited by thermal noise, with equal rms noise σ on a one and on a zero, the two levels must be separated by 2Qσ. The signal photocurrent is then about Qσ, giving the average power below.

blocks.where: P is the average received power in W; Q is the factor defined in chapter 4.6, about 6 at BER 10⁻⁹; σ is the rms noise current in A; R is the responsivity in A/W.

blocks.text: Practical PIN receivers reach about −25 to −40 dBm at a few hundred Mbit/s. An APD adds gain M before the preamplifier: the signal rises M times while the preamplifier noise stays fixed, buying roughly 5 to 10 dB. The gain needs a bias supply of tens of volts and a control loop against temperature drift, so an APD receiver costs more.

examples.question: A PIN receiver has responsivity R = 0.9 A/W and a total input noise current σ = 40 nA rms. It must reach BER 10⁻⁹, which needs Q = 6. (a) Find the sensitivity in watts and in dBm. (b) If the fiber and connectors lose 30 dB, what average power must the transmitter launch?
steps: Write the thermal-noise-limited sensitivity: P = Qσ/R.
Convert to dBm: 10 log₁₀(267 × 10⁻⁹ / 1 × 10⁻³) = 10 log₁₀(2.67 × 10⁻⁴) = −35.7 dBm.
Add the loss: launch power = −35.7 dBm + 30 dB = −5.7 dBm.
examples.answer: The sensitivity is 2.67 × 10⁻⁷ W (267 nW, −35.7 dBm), so a link with 30 dB of loss needs at least −5.7 dBm launched.
examples.check:
import math
Q = 6
sigma = 40e-9
R = 0.9
P = Q * sigma / R
P_nW = P * 1e9
P_dBm = 10 * math.log10(P / 1e-3)
launch = P_dBm + 30
print(round(P, 9))
print(round(P_nW, 1))
print(round(P_dBm, 1))
print(round(launch, 1))

traps: Quoting a sensitivity figure without the bit rate and the BER it was measured at. The same receiver is far less sensitive at a higher rate.
Mixing peak and average power. The formulas use average power; some datasheets quote peak.
Losing track of the dBm reference. 0 dBm is 1 mW, so −30 dBm is 1 µW, and every 10 dB is a factor of ten in power.
Assuming APD gain always helps. Past the optimum M the multiplied shot noise, which grows as M²F, outweighs the gain and sensitivity falls.
Adding noise currents directly. Independent noise currents add as squares: σ_total² = σ₁² + σ₂².

quiz.q: State the four jobs a receiver performs, in order.
quiz.a: Light-to-current conversion, low-noise amplification, pulse shaping with filtering, and a clocked decision between one and zero.

quiz.q: Why does a high-impedance front end need an equaliser?
quiz.a: A large load resistor with the input capacitance gives a narrow bandwidth of about 1/(2πR_L C). The equaliser boosts high frequencies to restore the pulse shape, which also boosts noise there and reduces dynamic range.

quiz.q: What must a sensitivity specification always state?
quiz.a: The bit rate and the bit error rate, plus whether the power is average or peak; for an APD, the gain as well.

quiz.q: A receiver has R = 0.8 A/W and σ = 50 nA rms, and Q = 6 at the target BER. Find its sensitivity in dBm.
In a transimpedance front end R_f is doubled. What happens to noise current and bandwidth, and when does the change help?
quiz.a: The thermal noise current falls by √2 because it scales as √(4kT/R_f), and the bandwidth halves because it scales as 1/(2πR_f C). It helps only if the halved bandwidth still passes the bit rate; otherwise the pulses smear and the eye closes.

quiz.q: Why does a receiver fail at very high input power?
quiz.a: The amplifiers overload and saturate, so the pulses flatten and the one and zero levels no longer separate at the threshold. This sets the upper end of the dynamic range.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production receivers integrate the photodiode, transimpedance stage and limiting amplifier on one die, and CMOS front ends are routine at 10 Gbit/s and above. Coherent receivers push the equaliser and clock recovery into digital signal processing as adaptive filters. The APD bias loop is a small control-systems problem in itself, since gain drifts with temperature. Useful search terms are transimpedance amplifier design, receiver overload, coherent DSP receiver and APD bias temperature compensation.
